items.title: Someone let Claude touch a 1994 Jeep's fuel system through its ECU
items.why: While reverse-engineering the ECU, Claude primed the fuel pump for about 10 seconds - agents are starting to touch hardware directly.

items.title: A DIY robot head that turns toward whoever's talking, Pi 5 + ESP32
items.why: Open-source MIT repo: a Pi 5 brain plus two ESP32-S3s for reflexes and expression - weekend build mixing Claude, Pi and microcontrollers.

items.title: An AI edited 0.016% of another model's weights and fixed its math score
items.why: GPT-6 Astra hand-edited a sliver of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights directly, no training - MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.
items.source: Simon Willison, on Takehi, Teoh, Zhang & Khattab

items.title: Postgres 19 can shrink a bloated table without locking it for reads
items.why: The new REPACK CONCURRENTLY rebuilds a table's file under a light lock instead of VACUUM FULL's full lock, reclaiming space live.

items.title: A newly disclosed Java bug, nicknamed Java4Shell, hits Jira and Jenkins
items.why: OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder heap-overflows on bad input, CVSS 9.2 - no patched build existed when the bug went public.

items.title: One reusable pattern makes lazy segment trees far less bug-prone
items.why: Define six small building blocks once, and any new range-update problem plugs into the same traversal code with no rewriting.

items.title: Brendan Gregg's rule: never trust a benchmark's own printed number
items.why: Watch vmstat, perf or eBPF while a benchmark actually runs - casual passive runs often measure the wrong bottleneck entirely.

items.title: Back-to-back hard training kept mice's dopamine system stuck high
items.why: Early mouse study: dopamine stayed elevated 48 hours after rest-free double sessions - give hard training real recovery time.

items.title: A 30-year cohort found a strength-training sweet spot near 100 min/week
items.why: Among 147k people, 90-119 minutes a week tracked with the lowest mortality - more wasn't better, nothing extra came past 120 minutes.
items.source: British Journal of Sports Medicine (via ScienceDaily)

items.title: Before a big interview, tell yourself you're excited, not calm
items.why: Harvard study: people told to say 'I'm excited' scored 8% higher on a hard math test, and hit 80% vs 53% on a timed task.
items.source: APA, on Alison Wood Brooks (Harvard Business School)
